title: AI for finance, lesson 5: reading financial statements with AI - the basics
subtitle: How to get AI to find revenue, profit, cash flow and borrowings.
whyItMatters: Being able to read these five figures and understand how they relate is already enough to spot most companies with an obvious financial problem.
openingQuestion: Which set of figures should a beginner start with when reading financial statements using AI?
openingOptions: Revenue, profit, operating cash flow, cash and borrowings
Every line in the notes to the accounts, all at once
Only the company logo printed on the report cover
Only the current share price quoted for the stock
explanation: Financial statements are a company's health record, and the safest way in for a beginner is five core figures: revenue, profit after tax, operating cash flow, cash and borrowings. AI can find those five in a couple of minutes instead of the half hour it takes to page through the document - but only if you force it to state the page number for each one. Without a source page you cannot tell a figure it read from a figure it inferred.

summary.keyIdea: Financial statements are a company's health record; AI finds the figures fast, but must cite its sources.
summary.commonMistake: Uploading the report and then asking vaguely 'is this company any good'.
summary.action: Use AI to extract the five basic figures and require a source page for each.

sections.text: A long set of financial statements is not intimidating if you start from a handful of core figures.
The five figures a beginner needs to find

sections.label: Terminology
sections.text: Financial statements: the company's reported accounts. Operating cash flow: the real cash generated by the main business. Borrowings: money the company has borrowed and must repay.
Read the attached report. Extract five figures: revenue, profit after tax, operating cash flow, cash, borrowings. Output a table with the columns Item, Value, Unit, Year, Source page.
Pick two of the figures at random and open the stated source page to verify them. If the page or the unit is wrong, send it back and make the model redo the work.

sections.title: The five figures and the question each one answers

concepts.def: How much the company sold in the period. It is the top line of the income statement. The three-year trend matters more than any single year.
What is left after all costs, interest and tax. This is the figure in the books, and not necessarily cash that has arrived.
Real cash collected from the main business. Found in the cash flow statement. If it diverges far from profit for several years, find out why.
How much money the company has ready to use. Found on the balance sheet, under current assets.
Total short-term and long-term borrowings. Put it next to cash and operating cash flow to see what the company would repay it with.

sections.text: Two comparisons to make as soon as you have the table

items: Operating cash flow against profit after tax: profit positive while cash flow is negative for several years running is a signal to dig deeper.
Borrowings against cash and operating cash flow: large debt is far less worrying than large debt with cash generation too small for the repayment obligation.

sections.label: A full prompt to reuse
sections.text: "Use only the attached financial statements. Build a table of 5 rows (revenue, profit after tax, cash flow from operating activities, cash and cash equivalents, total borrowings) × 3 columns for the most recent years. Note the page number and unit in every cell. State clearly whether these are consolidated or parent-company figures. Where you cannot find a figure, write 'Not found' - never estimate."
Three common errors when extracting figures with AI

items: Mixing consolidated with parent-company figures - the two tables sit next to each other in the same file and are very easy to confuse.
Mixing cumulative figures with single-quarter figures - especially in the Q2 and Q3 reports.
Mixing units - a report may present figures in dong, millions or billions in different tables.

sections.text: The AI catches none of these three on its own, because the output still reads as 'grammatically correct'. The only defence is to require page numbers and then open two of them yourself to cross-check. It takes two minutes, and those two minutes separate a table you can use from a table that merely looks right.

lines: Reading financial statements with AI starts from the basic figures.
The source page matters more than a nice-sounding answer.

quiz.question: When AI extracts figures from financial statements, what does the resulting table need?
options: The value and a comparison against the industry average
The value, the unit, the year and the source page
The value plus the AI's own assessment of it
The value along with a forecast for the following year
quiz.explanation: The source page and the unit are what let you check the figure. An industry comparison, an assessment or a forecast may all be useful later, but none of them can be verified against the document itself - and an unverified table is exactly what you were trying to avoid by extracting the numbers in the first place. Page references turn a twenty-figure table into twenty checks of a few seconds each.

quiz.question: Which question is too broad when reading financial statements with AI?
options: What was operating cash flow in 2025?
What was 2025 revenue, and on which page?
Is this company worth investing in?
Which page shows short-term borrowings?
quiz.explanation: A question that broad invites a vague answer. The other three each name a specific figure or a specific location in the document, so the answer can be checked against the page in seconds. 'Is it worth investing in' names nothing, cannot be verified, and invites the model to blend what it just read with what it half-remembers about the company - which is exactly the failure mode page references exist to catch.

quiz.question: A company reports steady profits but negative operating cash flow for several years. What does this usually suggest?
options: Depreciation expense in the period was far too large
The company is paying down its long-term borrowings
The company is growing extremely well right now
Receivables and inventory need to be checked
quiz.explanation: The gap between profit and cash flow is not by itself evidence of fraud, but it is always a question that has to be answered, and the place to look is usually receivables, inventory and the related notes. Large depreciation would push cash flow above profit rather than below it; repaying debt sits in financing rather than operating cash flow; and rapid growth does not on its own explain years of negative operating cash.

quiz.question: Which of the following errors can AI NOT detect on its own when extracting figures from a report?
options: Taking the parent-company figure instead of the consolidated one
Writing the unit down as millions when the report actually says billions
Adding up a column in the table and getting the total wrong
Skipping a row when extracting from a long multi-page table
quiz.explanation: Confusing consolidated with parent-company figures produces a table that is entirely valid in form and wrong in substance - nothing about it looks off. The other three leave traces that a careful reader or a second pass can catch: a unit that clashes with the figures beside it, a column total that does not add up, a missing row against a numbered list. Only checking the source page catches the first kind.

quiz.question: Why should every figure AI extracts from a report carry a page number or the line name from the original?
options: Because accounting standards require sources to be fully cited
Because it is the only quick way to check a figure was not misread
Because the AI computes more accurately when citing positions
Because the reader needs the page count to judge reliability
quiz.explanation: Checking a twenty-figure table with no sources means reading the whole report again. With a location attached, each figure takes seconds to confirm - that is the difference between a workflow you can actually use and one that merely sounds efficient. Presentation standards govern the company's own report rather than your extraction; the model does not compute better for citing; and the page count says nothing about reliability.

diagram.label: Profit after tax (what is left in the books)
Operating cash flow (how much real cash came in)
Cash and borrowings (how long it can hold out)

realWorldExample.company: When profit and cash flow part ways
realWorldExample.description: One of the classic situations in analysis: a company reports profits year after year while cash flow from operating activities stays negative. The gap usually sits in receivables and inventory - the company has recognised revenue without collecting the money, or paid for goods it has not sold. This is why the five-figure table must always show operating cash flow next to profit: looking at profit alone, you would see nothing unusual.

keyTakeaways: The five figures to start with: revenue, profit after tax, operating cash flow, cash, borrowings.
Always take at least 3 years or 3 periods - a single figure tells you nothing about the trend.
Make the AI cite a page number for every cell; where there is none, it must write 'Not found'.
Open two pages yourself to cross-check before using the table for anything else.
